title: Authentication and Authorization Fundamentals
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and terminology of Authentication and Authorization Fundamentals.
Apply or interpret one Express.js 5 pattern related to authentication versus authorization.
Identify a meaningful edge case and choose a repeatable local test for it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn authentication and authorization fundamentals and connect the named syllabus points to a small Express.js example. The course baseline is Express 5.x on a supported Node.js LTS release; the page shows reference output, not execution of Node.js code.
content.why_it_matters: Authentication and Authorization Fundamentals matters because it helps keep the request/response contract explicit and the application maintainable as inputs, users and dependencies become less predictable. Identity plus server-side permission checks.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Authentication and Authorization Fundamentals is part of authentication, authorization, and sessions. Authentication answers who is making a request; authorization answers what that identity may do. Hash passwords with established libraries, enforce access on the server, and design sessions/tokens for expiration and revocation. For this topic, make the observable behavior explicit, then check what happens when an input is missing, malformed, unauthorized, or a dependency fails (choose the relevant cases for this lesson).

items.title: Authentication versus authorization
items.text: Authentication verifies an identity. Store password hashes with an established password-hashing library, rate-limit sensitive endpoints, and never log or return credentials.

items.title: Anonymous and authenticated requests
items.text: Connect this syllabus point to Authentication and Authorization Fundamentals: state the expected behavior, identify a realistic edge case, and choose a test or observation that proves the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

items.title: Users, roles, and permissions
items.text: Authorization checks what the verified identity may do. Enforce permissions and resource ownership in the server for every protected operation; hiding a button is not access control.

items.title: Public and protected resources
items.text: Keep the interface predictable for its client: use clear resource boundaries, explicit request/response formats, correct status codes, validation and tests for failure cases.

content_blocks.title: Read the example carefully
content_blocks.text: A useful way to study authentication and authorization fundamentals is to start from the first syllabus point — authentication versus authorization — and follow it through a small request or application example. Keep Express's built-in behavior separate from optional packages and your own application policy.

content_blocks.title: Worked example (reference only)
content_blocks.expected_output: Registration stores a password hash. Login compares the submitted password with the stored hash; the actual account/session flow remains application-specific.
content_blocks.notes: Use a maintained password-hashing library and apply rate limits. This fragment needs to be inside an async function and requires the bcrypt package.

content_blocks.title: Safety / production rule
content_blocks.text: Module rule — Authentication answers who is making a request; authorization answers what that identity may do. Hash passwords with established libraries, enforce access on the server, and design sessions/tokens for expiration and revocation.

content.task: Try it yourself: adapt the worked example to demonstrate authentication and authorization fundamentals. Write down the exact request or command, expected status/body, one boundary case, and how you would reset the local lab. CodeLeaf does not execute Express code in this lesson page; run Node.js server examples locally.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example has a clear local run or inspection path and the required dependencies are named.
A normal request and a malformed/edge/failure request have documented expected outcomes.
No credentials, production data, or claim of successful runtime execution is included.
hints: Hint 1: identify which part of authentication and authorization fundamentals is supplied by Express and which part belongs to your own application or another package.
Hint 2: check the official Express 5 guide/API reference and isolate the smallest example that proves one behavior.
Hint 3: verify a success case, a boundary case and the expected status/response; restart from a clean state before repeating.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: Authentication answers who is making a request; authorization answers what that identity may do. Hash passwords with established libraries, enforce access on the server, and design sessions/tokens for expiration and revocation. The sample is a focused reference fragment. Review all dependency, schema, proxy and runtime assumptions before using it in an application.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying an example without checking its assumptions
common_mistakes.why: A fragment may omit route setup, middleware order, external packages, database schema or production configuration.
common_mistakes.fix: State the runtime/dependency assumptions, run the focused example locally, and test a success path plus one failure path.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating all request values as trusted
common_mistakes.why: Parameters, query values, body properties, files and upstream responses can be missing or malicious.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate schema, type and bounds at the boundary; keep authorization and database constraints as separate checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the demo output means the server executed
common_mistakes.why: The course page shows reference output for Node.js/Express code; it is not an isolated Node runtime.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example locally with the documented Node.js version and record actual command/output and test results.

summary: Explain the central idea behind authentication and authorization fundamentals.
Connect the relevant subtopics to the request/response or application boundary.
Verify one normal outcome and one edge/error case with repeatable evidence.
run_instructions: Open a terminal in the lesson lab directory.
Install dependencies for the sample if required; use a supported Node.js LTS release.
Run the documented file with node, send the stated request with curl or an API client, and compare the actual status/body with the reference.
reset_steps: Stop the local process with Ctrl+C.
Clear only temporary/synthetic records or files created by the lab.
Restart the server before repeating the example.
troubleshooting: If node reports a module-syntax error, check package.json module type or use the matching CommonJS syntax.
If a package cannot be resolved, install the named dependency in the local lab and verify the lockfile.
If output differs, verify middleware order, the request path/method, environment variables and the expected runtime version.
